He told himself it was the hour, that the shop was open and a man does not leave his counter for a mark on the road, but there was no one in the shop and had not been since Thursday. He stayed behind the glass and watched the place where she had crouched until the light changed and he could no longer be sure which patch was print and which was only the tar drying unevenly, the way it did.

At four he took the card out from under the envelope and read it again. A pound of nails. The figure was correct to the penny, and he had not changed it in three years, and it was not written on any sign. He had it in a ledger in the back room in his own hand. He went and looked at the ledger. The page was there. Nothing was disturbed.

The man from the van had come on the Tuesday. He had laid the strip without asking, without a word to anyone on the street, and then knelt and put his palm to it as if it were a thing he had made himself and was proud of. He had looked up at the shop while he did it. Not at the window. At the shop, the whole face of it, the way a surveyor looks.

He put the card back. Two lines, a price, a hand on the road. He counted them on his fingers, and then, not liking that, stopped."}
